docs.title: Migrating from v0.2 to v0.3
docs.text: v0.3 keeps the draft -11 wire format, so v0.2 and v0.3 parties interoperate. It verifies more strictly and changes some server APIs. The root package changes little; most changes are in personserver, accessserver and agentprovider.

docs.title: 1. ResourceGuard binds requests to its resource and its access server
docs.text:
ResourceGuardConfig.Resource must be a URL with a host: the guard refuses a request signed for another host. In four-party mode (Audience set to the access server), an auth token must be issued by that access server; TrustIssuer no longer admits it, and needs to list only person servers.

// v0.2: TrustIssuer listed the PS and the AS
guard, err := aauth.NewResourceGuard(aauth.ResourceGuardConfig{
    Resource: "https://files.example", Audience: "https://as.example",
    TrustIssuer: aauth.TrustIssuers("https://ps.example", "https://as.example"),
})

// v0.3: auth tokens come from Audience; TrustIssuer covers person tokens
guard, err := aauth.NewResourceGuard(aauth.ResourceGuardConfig{
    Resource: "https://files.example", Audience: "https://as.example",
    TrustIssuer: aauth.TrustIssuers("https://ps.example"),
})

The guard now applies Verify.Signature to agent-token requests too and verifies agent tokens with the strict provider profile unless Verify.InsecureSkipIdentifierCheck is set. New: Caller.AgentIssuer, Caller.Account, Caller.Tenant, Caller.JTI and ResourceGuardConfig.IsRevoked.

docs.title: 2. AuthorizationHandler requires TrustIssuer
docs.text:
Without it every person-token request is answered 500.

h := &aauth.AuthorizationHandler{
    // ...as before
    TrustIssuer: aauth.TrustIssuers("https://ps.example"),
}

docs.title: 3. Agent identifiers must be in their provider's domain
docs.text: VerifyAgentToken refuses an agent token whose sub domain is not the host of its iss, and NewAgent refuses such a self-hosted agent. Without RequireProviderClaims, an iss on a loopback host may still name agents of any domain, for local tests. agentprovider.New refuses a Config.Domain other than the issuer's host; leave it empty to use the issuer's host.

docs.title: 4. SelfSignedResolver verifies only top-level agent tokens
docs.text: Use JWKSResolver or StaticResolver for person, auth, resource and sub-agent tokens.

docs.title: 5. Verifying requests yourself
docs.text:
Set RequestVerifyOptions.Authority to your own host so a request signed for another server is refused:

authority, err := aauth.AuthorityOf("https://files.example")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
err = aauth.VerifyRequestWithOptions(req, pub, aauth.RequestVerifyOptions{Authority: authority})

Verification reads at most DefaultMaxVerifyBodyBytes (4 MiB) of a body; set MaxBodySize for more, or a negative value for no limit. Covered components with the tr or req parameter are refused. SignRequest covers @query when the URL has one, and SignRequestCovering covers extra components.

Other root-package changes callers may notice:

  • VerifyAgentTokenOptions.MaxLifetime (24 h by default) and ResourceTokenVerifyOptions.MaxLifetime (5 minutes by default) refuse longer-lived tokens.
  • WriteSignatureFailure and WriteTokenError no longer copy error text into the problem detail. Log the error yourself if you need it; TokenError.Detail returns the text that is safe to send.
  • Discovery refuses a dwk other than the four AAuth metadata documents (ValidateDWK) and redirects to another host (CheckSameHostRedirect). A client you pass instead of DiscoveryClient should do the same.
  • JWK.PublicKey refuses non-canonical base64url.

docs.title: 6. Person server approvals carry the revision shown
docs.text:
Grant.Revision is the Pending.Revision of the request the person saw. Approve fails with ErrRequestChanged when the agent replaced the request after it was shown. A zero revision approves only a request that was never updated.

// v0.2
err := ps.Approve(ctx, p.ID, personserver.Grant{Person: person})

// v0.3: pass the revision of the request the page showed
err := ps.Approve(ctx, p.ID, personserver.Grant{Person: person, Revision: p.Revision})

docs.title: 7. Interaction codes are looked up, then consumed at the decision
docs.text:
ConsumeCodeFor is removed. LookupCode shows the request without consuming the code, so a link preview cannot burn it; ConsumeCode takes the client key used for rate limiting (the browser's session or address) and the authenticated person.

// v0.2
p, err := ps.ConsumeCodeFor(ctx, code, clientIP)

// v0.3: show the request...
p, err := ps.LookupCode(ctx, code, clientIP)
// ...and when the signed-in person decides
p, err = ps.ConsumeCode(ctx, code, clientIP, person)

accessserver.Server has the same LookupCode and ConsumeCode.

docs.title: 8. ClaimsProvider takes a request
docs.text:
The provider learns which access server receives the claims, and for which resource, scope, mission and agent, so it can apply a release policy.

// v0.2
ClaimsProvider: func(ctx context.Context, person string, required []string) (map[string]any, error) {
    return lookupClaims(person, required)
},

// v0.3
ClaimsProvider: func(ctx context.Context, r *personserver.ClaimsRequest) (map[string]any, error) {
    return lookupClaims(r.Person, r.Required)
},

docs.title: 9. Call chaining is opt-in
docs.text: Set personserver.Config.AllowCallChaining to accept an upstream_token. Without it, chained requests are refused before the Decider runs. With it, a Decider should check TokenRequest.Chained; see the servers guide.

docs.title: 10. Access server approvals carry the revision
docs.text:
// v0.2
err := as.Approve(ctx, p.ID, scope)

// v0.3
err := as.Approve(ctx, p.ID, p.Revision, scope)

docs.title: 11. Stores gain pruning and counts
docs.text:
Your own Store implementations need:

  • personserver: Store.Prune(ctx, cutoff), TokenStore.CountRevocations(ctx, iss) and PendingStore.CountOpenPending(ctx, agent). CreatePending must refuse a duplicate interaction code with ErrCodeInUse.
  • accessserver: Store.CountRevocations(ctx, iss), Store.CountOpenPending(ctx, ps) and Store.Prune(ctx, cutoff). CreatePending and UpdatePending must refuse a duplicate code.

The servers call Prune every Config.PruneInterval (1 minute; negative turns it off) and cap open pending requests (MaxPendingPerAgent, MaxPendingPerPS) and revocations per issuer (MaxRevocationsPerIssuer), answering 429 past them. Pending URLs answer 410 Gone once their result was delivered, and the stored result is discarded.

docs.title: 12. Sandbox
docs.text:
• serve listens on 127.0.0.1:443 by default and refuses another interface without --listen-any-interface. The Docker image and Compose files pass it.
  • The signing helper signs only for the sandbox's hosts, --remote origins and upstreams; --signer-any-target lifts this, and --signer-host adds names it answers to.
  • The CA is replaced on the first run, because the old one has no name constraints. Trust the new ca.pem again in each tool.
  • In the sandbox package, LoadOrCreateCA(dir, domains...) takes the domains the CA may sign for (default aauth.test); existing calls compile. Signer gained a slice field (Hosts), so it can no longer be compared with ==.

docs.title: Migrating from v0.1 to v0.2
docs.text:
v0.1 implemented AAuth draft -09 with signature-key-04 and bootstrap-01. v0.2 implements draft -11 with signature-key-09 and bootstrap-02. Draft -11 changes the wire format, so v0.1 and v0.2 parties cannot talk to each other: upgrade every agent, resource, and server you operate together.

This guide lists every breaking change to the root aauth package, grouped by area, with before and after code. The personserver, accessserver, agentprovider, and ratelimit packages are new in v0.2 and have nothing to migrate. See the changelog for additions.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Module path
  • Keys and algorithms (1–8)
  • Signatures and Signature-Error (9–15)
  • Identifiers and common token rules (16–18)
  • Resource tokens (19–22)
  • Auth tokens (23–26)
  • PS client and metadata (27–32)
  • Missions (33–36)
  • Transport (37–38)
  • Delegation (39–40)

docs.title: Module path
docs.text:
The repository was renamed from auth-go to aauth-go, and v0.2 has the module path github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go. Update imports and go.mod:

// v0.1
import aauth "github.com/aauth-dev/auth-go"

// v0.2
import aauth "github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go"

go get github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go@v0.2.0

Subpackages move the same way, for example github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go/personserver. v0.1 releases remain available under the old path.

docs.title: 1. Agent.Priv and Agent.Pub are replaced by Agent.Key
docs.text:
Keys are crypto.Signers, so hardware-backed keys work. The public key is Agent.Key.Public().

// v0.1
sig := ed25519.Sign(agent.Priv, msg)
pub := agent.Pub

// v0.2
pub := agent.Key.Public()          // crypto.PublicKey
jwk := agent.JWK()                 // as before

docs.title: 2. WithKey takes a crypto.Signer
docs.text:
// v0.1
agent, err := aauth.NewAgent(id, aauth.WithKey(priv)) // ed25519.PrivateKey

// v0.2: any Ed25519 or P-256 crypto.Signer (ed25519.PrivateKey still works)
agent, err := aauth.NewAgent(id, aauth.WithKey(signer))
// or generate a P-256 key:
agent, err := aauth.NewAgent(id, aauth.WithKeyAlgorithm(aauth.AlgES256))

docs.title: 3. MintAgentToken, MintAuthToken, and MintResourceToken take a crypto.Signer
docs.text:
// v0.1
tok, err := aauth.MintAgentToken(claims, priv, kid) // priv ed25519.PrivateKey

// v0.2
tok, err := aauth.MintAgentToken(claims, key, kid) // key crypto.Signer

The JWS alg follows the key: Ed25519 or ES256.

docs.title: 4. SignRequest takes a crypto.Signer
docs.text:
// v0.1
err := aauth.SignRequest(req, agent.Priv, "sig")

// v0.2
err := aauth.SignRequest(req, agent.Key, "sig")

docs.title: 5. VerifyRequest takes a crypto.PublicKey
docs.text:
// v0.1
err := aauth.VerifyRequest(req, pub) // ed25519.PublicKey

// v0.2
err := aauth.VerifyRequest(req, pub) // crypto.PublicKey (ed25519.PublicKey or *ecdsa.PublicKey)
// with a validity window, clock, or required components:
err := aauth.VerifyRequestWithOptions(req, pub, aauth.RequestVerifyOptions{})

docs.title: 6. KeyResolver.ResolveKey returns crypto.PublicKey
docs.text:
Custom resolvers change their return type. The built-in JWKSResolver, StaticResolver, and SelfSignedResolver already do.

// v0.1
func (r myResolver) ResolveKey(ctx context.Context, iss, dwk, kid string, cnf *aauth.JWK) (ed25519.PublicKey, error)

// v0.2
func (r myResolver) ResolveKey(ctx context.Context, iss, dwk, kid string, cnf *aauth.JWK) (crypto.PublicKey, error)

A resolver that caches keys can also implement aauth.KeyRefresher, so verifiers refresh once when an issuer re-keys under the same kid.

docs.title: 7. JWK.PublicKey returns crypto.PublicKey and validates alg first
docs.text:
// v0.1
pub, err := jwk.PublicKey() // ed25519.PublicKey

// v0.2
pub, err := jwk.PublicKey() // crypto.PublicKey; ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm or ErrInvalidKey for a bad alg
edPub, ok := pub.(ed25519.PublicKey)

docs.title: 8. JWS and JWK alg is Ed25519, not EdDSA (wire change)
docs.text:
Tokens and keys are minted with the fully-specified Ed25519 algorithm. Tokens or keys using EdDSA, none, a symmetric algorithm, or no alg are rejected, as are keys whose kty/crv disagree with alg or that omit crv. Republish any hand-written JWKS with "alg": "Ed25519" (or "ES256"); aauth.NewJWK and Agent.JWKS produce conforming keys.

// v0.1
{"kty": "OKP", "crv": "Ed25519", "x": "...", "alg": "EdDSA"}

// v0.2
{"kty": "OKP", "crv": "Ed25519", "x": "...", "alg": "Ed25519"}

docs.title: 9. WriteSignatureError no longer takes a status code
docs.text:
Every signature failure is a 401. Most servers should call WriteSignatureFailure, which picks the code from the error.

// v0.1
aauth.WriteSignatureError(w, http.StatusUnauthorized, aauth.SignatureError{Code: aauth.SigErrInvalidSignature}, "bad signature")

// v0.2
aauth.WriteSignatureError(w, aauth.SignatureError{Code: aauth.SigErrInvalidSignature}, "bad signature")
// or, from any verification error:
aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err)

docs.title: 10. SigErrKeyNotFound is replaced by SigErrUnknownKey (wire change)
docs.text:
The code is now unknown_key, from the signature-key-09 registry. A kid missing from a JWKS or pinned key set is aauth.ErrUnknownKey.

// v0.1
if se.Code == aauth.SigErrKeyNotFound { ... }

// v0.2
if se.Code == aauth.SigErrUnknownKey { ... }

docs.title: 11. SigErrExpiredSignature is removed (wire change)
docs.text:
signature-key-09 has no expired_signature. An expired token is expired_jwt (SigErrExpiredJWT); a signature whose created is older than the validity window is invalid_signature; one ahead of the verifier's clock is clock_skew (SigErrClockSkew).

// v0.1
case aauth.SigErrExpiredSignature:

// v0.2
case aauth.SigErrExpiredJWT, aauth.SigErrClockSkew:

The other new codes are unsupported_scheme, cache_miss, invalid_request, issuer_missing, issuer_mismatch, invalid_jwt, and revoked_jwt.

docs.title: 12. Signature-Error is an RFC 9651 dictionary (wire change)
docs.text:
SignatureError.String serializes a Structured Field Dictionary (string parameters quoted, required_input as an inner list of strings), and ParseSignatureError parses one, rejecting malformed values instead of splitting on commas. invalid_input exposes its components as SignatureError.RequiredInput, and unsupported_scheme / unsupported_algorithm responses carry Accept-Signature-Scheme / Accept-Signature-Alg (AcceptSignatureFromResponse).

Signature-Error: error=invalid_input, required_input=("content-digest" "content-type")

docs.title: 13. Signature-Key is parsed as a dictionary keyed by label (wire change)
docs.text: Only the member for the verified label is read. A scheme other than jwt at an agent endpoint is unsupported_scheme (ErrUnsupportedScheme), answered with Accept-Signature-Scheme. AttachSignatureKey emits the canonical serialization. Code that only calls AttachSignatureKey and ParseSignatureKey needs no change.

docs.title: 14. Signature created is enforced and coverage changed (wire change)
docs.text:
Verification no longer skips the created check: a signature must be created within the validity window (default 60 seconds, aauth.DefaultSignatureWindow, or a resource's signature_window). Requests with a body cover content-type as well as content-digest, and the keyid signature parameter is no longer sent. Keep clocks synchronized; to widen the window at a verifier:

claims, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractAgent(ctx, req, aauth.VerifyAgentTokenOptions{
    Resolver:  resolver,
    Signature: aauth.RequestVerifyOptions{Window: 2 * time.Minute},
})

docs.title: 15. ParseRequirement requires an RFC 9651 dictionary (wire change)
docs.text:
A requirement given as a quoted string is rejected; the requirement member must be a Token.

// v0.1 accepted
AAuth-Requirement: requirement="auth-token"; resource-token="..."

// v0.2
AAuth-Requirement: requirement=auth-token; resource-token="..."

Use ChallengeAgentToken, ChallengePersonToken, ChallengeAuthToken, or Requirement.String to produce conforming values.

docs.title: 16. Agent identifiers are validated per draft -11 §5.2
docs.text: ParseAgentIdentifier rejects local parts outside A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ + . or longer than 255 characters, malformed sub-agent names, and domains that are not lowercase A-label host names (no scheme, port, or path). Failures wrap aauth.ErrInvalidIdentifier. Identifiers remain case-sensitive.

docs.title: 17. Server-issued tokens follow the common JWT rules (draft -11 §11.5)
docs.text:
iat is required, exp has no skew tolerance, iss must be a server identifier (https, host only, lowercase), typ and dwk are checked first, person and auth tokens may not live longer than one hour, and every token must carry jti. Agent tokens verified with RequireProviderClaims also require server-identifier iss and ps. For local development against http://127.0.0.1:port servers, set InsecureSkipIdentifierCheck in the verify options; never in production.

Discovery with no client configured now uses aauth.DiscoveryClient, which reaches only public https destinations. Against local servers, pass a client to NewJWKSResolver, FetchMetadata, RevocationClient, and each server's Config.HTTPClient.

docs.title: 18. Metadata documents must carry a matching issuer
docs.text: FetchMetadata (and every resolver built on it) rejects a document with no issuer (ErrIssuerMissing) or whose issuer differs from the URL it was fetched under (ErrIssuerMismatch). Publish issuer in every aauth-*.json you serve.

docs.title: 19. IssueResourceToken takes ResourceTokenParams and a verified presented token
docs.text:
A resource token can only be issued against a verified person token or auth token; its ps, sub, jti, mission_s256, and tenant are copied from it. Without one, answer requirement=person-token.

// v0.1
rt, err := aauth.IssueResourceToken(resourceURL, psURL, agentClaims, "files:read", priv, kid)

// v0.2
person, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractPerson(ctx, req, resourceURL, verifyOpts)
if err != nil {
    aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err)
    return
}
rt, err := aauth.IssueResourceToken(aauth.ResourceTokenParams{
    Resource: resourceURL,
    Scope:    "files:read",
    // Audience: the access server, for four-party; empty means the person's PS.
}, person, key, kid)

docs.title: 20. VerifyResourceToken takes ResourceTokenVerifyOptions and returns the presented token
docs.text:
// v0.1
rc, err := aauth.VerifyResourceToken(ctx, token, audience, agentClaims, resolver)

// v0.2
rc, presented, err := aauth.VerifyResourceToken(ctx, token, aauth.ResourceTokenVerifyOptions{
    TokenVerifyOptions: aauth.TokenVerifyOptions{Resolver: resolver},
    Audience:           audience,
    PS:                 psIssuer,
    AgentJKT:           agentClaims.Cnf.JWK.Thumbprint(),
    PresentedToken:     req.PresentedToken,
})

Failures are *aauth.TokenErrors with the §11.9.3 codes.

docs.title: 21. VerifyResourceChallenge takes a context and ResourceChallengeOptions
docs.text:
It now verifies the resource token's signature and checks ps, sub, and presented_jti against the token the agent presented. Transport does this for you.

// v0.1
rc, err := aauth.VerifyResourceChallenge(token, resourceURL, agent)

// v0.2
rc, err := aauth.VerifyResourceChallenge(ctx, token, aauth.ResourceChallengeOptions{
    TokenVerifyOptions: aauth.TokenVerifyOptions{Resolver: aauth.NewJWKSResolver(hc)},
    Resource:           resourceURL,
    Agent:              agent,
    PS:                 psIssuer,
    Presented:          presentedToken,
})

docs.title: 22. ResourceClaims drops Agent and Mission (wire change)
docs.text:
A resource token no longer names the agent; agent_jkt binds it to the agent's key. New members: PS, PresentedJTI, MissionS256, Account, LoginHint, and Tenant.

// v0.1
who := rc.Agent
mission := rc.Mission.S256

// v0.2
mission := rc.MissionS256
ps, sub := rc.PS, rc.Subject // the person, as a directed identifier at that PS

docs.title: 23. AuthClaims drops Agent, Act, and Mission (wire change)
docs.text:
An auth token carries no agent identifier and no delegation chain. It now carries the REQUIRED ps and a directed sub, plus optional account and mission_s256.

// v0.1
agentID := ac.Agent
mission := ac.Mission.S256

// v0.2
ps, sub := ac.PS, ac.Subject
mission := ac.MissionS256

docs.title: 24. ActClaim, ActClaim.Delegators, and NextAct are removed
docs.text: Draft -11 removed act. There is no replacement; call chaining is carried by upstream_token (see Delegation).

docs.title: 25. VerifyAuthToken and VerifyAndExtractAuth take AuthTokenVerifyOptions
docs.text:
// v0.1
ac, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractAuth(ctx, req, resourceURL, resolver)

// v0.2
ac, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractAuth(ctx, req, resourceURL, aauth.AuthTokenVerifyOptions{
    TokenVerifyOptions: aauth.TokenVerifyOptions{Resolver: resolver},
    CheckSubject:       nil, // optional (iss, sub) record check, §9.4.3.2
})

docs.title: 26. Auth and person token cnf and ps are checked more strictly
docs.text: Auth and person tokens must carry a structurally complete cnf.jwk that passes algorithm validation, and a PS-issued auth token must have ps equal to iss. Tokens minted by v0.1 issuers fail these checks.

docs.title: 27. TokenRequest, TokenResponse, and ExchangeToken are renamed
docs.text:
They are AuthTokenRequest, AuthTokenResponse, and PSClient.RequestAuthToken. The optional request parameters move into the embedded TokenRequestHints, and PresentedToken (the token the agent presented to the resource) is REQUIRED.

// v0.1
res, err := ps.ExchangeToken(ctx, aauth.TokenRequest{
    ResourceToken: rt,
    Justification: "list files",
})

// v0.2
res, err := ps.RequestAuthToken(ctx, aauth.AuthTokenRequest{
    ResourceToken:     rt,
    PresentedToken:    presented, // ErrPresentedTokenMissing if empty
    TokenRequestHints: aauth.TokenRequestHints{Justification: "list files"},
})

docs.title: 28. PSClient.TokenEndpoint is PSClient.AuthTokenEndpoint
docs.text:
// v0.1
ps.TokenEndpoint = "https://ps.example/token"

// v0.2
ps.AuthTokenEndpoint = "https://ps.example/token"
ps.PersonTokenEndpoint = "https://ps.example/person"
// or fill every endpoint from the PS metadata:
_, err := ps.Discover(ctx)

docs.title: 29. token_endpoint is auth_token_endpoint in PS metadata (wire change)
docs.text: PersonServerMetadata.TokenEndpoint is AuthTokenEndpoint, and person_token_endpoint (PersonTokenEndpoint) is REQUIRED. PersonServerMetadata.Validate reports missing members.

docs.title: 30. Metadata types embed ServerMetadata
docs.text:
Issuer and JWKSURI (and the display members) moved to an embedded ServerMetadata in AgentProviderMetadata, PersonServerMetadata, and ResourceMetadata. Field access is unchanged; composite literals name the embedded struct. issuer is no longer omitempty.

// v0.1
md := aauth.ResourceMetadata{Issuer: self, JWKSURI: self + "/jwks"}

// v0.2
md := aauth.ResourceMetadata{
    ServerMetadata: aauth.ServerMetadata{Issuer: self, JWKSURI: self + "/jwks"},
}

docs.title: 31. Clarification updated requests carry presented_token
docs.text:
ClarificationReply.PresentedToken is REQUIRED for an updated_request, and the client refuses one without it. On the server side, ParseClarificationPost returns a *TokenError (invalid_request) for a malformed body or an updated_request lacking resource_token or presented_token.

// v0.1
return aauth.ClarificationReply{ResourceToken: newRT}, nil

// v0.2
return aauth.ClarificationReply{ResourceToken: newRT, PresentedToken: presented}, nil

docs.title: 32. Token endpoints report a terminated mission as *MissionStatusError
docs.text:
RequestPersonToken, PersonToken, and RequestAuthToken return a *aauth.MissionStatusError (not a *TokenError) when the request names a mission that is no longer active, as the other PS endpoints already did.

var mse *aauth.MissionStatusError
if errors.As(err, &mse) {
    // stop acting on the mission; mse.TerminationReason says why
}

docs.title: 33. MissionRef is replaced by mission_s256 (wire change)
docs.text:
A mission is identified by its PS and its s256, sent as a single mission_s256 string.

// v0.1
req := aauth.PermissionRequest{Action: "SendEmail", Mission: &aauth.MissionRef{Approver: psURL, S256: s256}}

// v0.2
req := aauth.PermissionRequest{Action: "SendEmail", MissionS256: s256}

docs.title: 34. AuditRequest.Mission is AuditRequest.MissionS256 and is REQUIRED
docs.text:
// v0.1
err := ps.Audit(ctx, aauth.AuditRequest{Mission: aauth.MissionRef{Approver: psURL, S256: s256}, Action: "SendEmail"})

// v0.2
err := ps.Audit(ctx, aauth.AuditRequest{MissionS256: s256, Action: "SendEmail"})

docs.title: 35. WriteMissionStatusError is replaced by WriteMissionTerminated
docs.text:
A mission is either active or terminated; the response carries an optional termination reason.

// v0.1
aauth.WriteMissionStatusError(w, "revoked")

// v0.2
aauth.WriteMissionTerminated(w, aauth.TerminationRevoked)

docs.title: 36. Mission status errors carry termination_reason (wire change)
docs.text: MissionStatusError.MissionStatus is always terminated; the reason is in TerminationReason (completed, revoked, expired, superseded, administrative, or an unrecognized value kept as-is).

docs.title: 37. Transport.ExpiryLeeway is Transport.RefreshMargin
docs.text:
The default margin is five minutes (aauth.DefaultRefreshMargin): a cached token with less time left is not presented again.

// v0.1
tr.ExpiryLeeway = 30 * time.Second

// v0.2
tr.RefreshMargin = 5 * time.Minute

docs.title: 38. Transport answers requirement=person-token
docs.text: A Transport with a PSClient now obtains a person token instead of returning an error for requirement=person-token, and verifies resource token challenges against the PS client's issuer rather than the agent token's ps claim. Discover the PS (PSClient.Discover) or set its endpoints explicitly.

docs.title: 39. Agent.MintSubAgentToken is removed
docs.text:
A sub-agent holds its own key, and its token is issued by the parent's agent provider. Sub-agent tokens are no longer verifiable with SelfSignedResolver; verify them against the parent's provider keys.

// v0.1
tok, err := parent.MintSubAgentToken("worker-1")

// v0.2: generate the sub-agent and its key together
sub, err := parent.NewSubAgent("worker-1")
// or issue a token for a key held elsewhere
tok, err := parent.IssueSubAgentToken("worker-1", subKey.Public())

A sub-agent requests authorization through its parent: aauth.NewTransport(sub, parentPSClient) sends subagent_token.

docs.title: 40. RouteDownstream takes a PresentedToken and routes by person server
docs.text:
Call chaining routes by the upstream token's person server: the iss of a person token or the ps of an auth token. ChainRouter.Endpoint and Governed are replaced by PersonServer, MissionS256, and UpstreamExpiresAt, and ChainRouter.Transport builds the intermediary's transport.

// v0.1
r, err := aauth.RouteDownstream(upstreamAuthClaims, rawUpstream, isPS)
psc := aauth.NewPSClient(r.Endpoint, intermediary)

// v0.2
r, err := aauth.RouteDownstream(upstreamClaims, rawUpstream) // *PersonClaims or *AuthClaims
tr, err := r.Transport(intermediary)                          // intermediary must be its own agent provider
hc := &http.Client{Transport: tr}

docs.title: Resource
docs.text:
A resource verifies whichever token a request presents and challenges for the next one. With PS authorization (three-party), an agent token is answered with requirement=person-token, a person token with a resource token challenge (requirement=auth-token), and an auth token is served:

const self = "https://files.example" // the resource's server identifier
verify := aauth.TokenVerifyOptions{
    Resolver: aauth.NewJWKSResolver(nil), // nil: aauth.DiscoveryClient
    // Refuse a request the agent signed for another server.
    Signature: aauth.RequestVerifyOptions{Authority: "files.example"},
}

// A valid signature proves the issuer signed the claims, not that this
// resource should trust that issuer or its subjects. Token issuers are URLs
// the request chooses, so accept only the person servers you have chosen to
// trust, and key your own records by (iss, sub): sub is unique only within
// its issuer (§9.4.3.2). In three-party, auth tokens come from those person
// servers (dwk aauth-person.json); with an access server, only from it.
trusted := map[string]bool{"https://ps.example": true}
checkSubject := func(ctx context.Context, iss, sub string) error {
    if !trusted[iss] {
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: %s is not an issuer this resource accepts", aauth.ErrInvalidToken, iss)
    }
    return nil // or look up (iss, sub) in your own records
}

handler := func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    tok, err := aauth.ParseSignatureKey(r)
    if err != nil {
        aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err) // 401 with Signature-Error
        return
    }
    typ, err := aauth.TokenType(tok)
    if err != nil {
        aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err)
        return
    }
    switch typ {
    case aauth.TypAuth:
        claims, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractAuth(r.Context(), r, self,
            aauth.AuthTokenVerifyOptions{TokenVerifyOptions: verify, CheckSubject: checkSubject})
        if err != nil {
            aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err)
            return
        }
        if claims.DWK != aauth.WellKnownPerson { // from a PS, so ps is iss
            aauth.WriteProblem(w, http.StatusForbidden, aauth.ErrCodeInvalidRequest, "auth tokens are accepted from person servers only")
            return
        }
        // The identity is (iss, sub), never sub alone. The granted scope is
        // the issuer's claim: apply your own policy to it before acting.
        serve(w, claims.Issuer, claims.Subject, claims.Scope)
    case aauth.TypPerson:
        person, err := aauth.VerifyAndExtractPerson(r.Context(), r, self, verify)
        if err != nil {
            aauth.WriteSignatureFailure(w, err)
            return
        }
        if !trusted[person.Issuer] {
            aauth.WriteProblem(w, http.StatusForbidden, aauth.ErrCodeInvalidRequest, "person server not accepted")
            return
        }
        rt, err := aauth.IssueResourceToken(
            aauth.ResourceTokenParams{Resource: self, Scope: "files:read"},
            person, resourceKey, resourceKID)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        aauth.ChallengeAuthToken(w, rt) // 401 requirement=auth-token
    default:
        aauth.ChallengePersonToken(w) // 401 requirement=person-token
    }
}

In four-party mode, accept auth tokens only from the resource's own access server (iss equal to it, dwk aauth-access.json), never from a person server, and restrict which scopes it may grant (draft -11 §13.7). The resource also serves /.well-known/aauth-resource.json (aauth.ResourceMetadata) and the JWKS holding resourceKey. A resource that needs only the agent's identity stops at aauth.VerifyAndExtractAgent. For four-party access, set ResourceTokenParams.Audience to the resource's access server. The compile-checked version is Example_resource.

docs.title: Protect Operations with ResourceGuard
docs.text:
Most resources need different levels for different operations: reading a catalog needs only the agent's identity, an order needs the person, and a change needs the person's consent for a scope. aauth.ResourceGuard writes the switch above once. Each operation declares the least it requires, and the guard verifies the presented token, answers with the next requirement when it falls short, and passes the verified caller to the handler:

guard, err := aauth.NewResourceGuard(aauth.ResourceGuardConfig{
    Resource:    self,                      // aud of the tokens it accepts
    Key:         resourceKey,               // signs resource tokens
    Verify:      verify,                    // PS and AS keys
    TrustIssuer: aauth.TrustIssuers("https://ps.example"),
    Metadata:    aauth.ResourceMetadata{AccessMode: aauth.AccessModeAuthToken},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.Handle("GET /pets", guard.Require(aauth.Access{Level: aauth.AccessAgent}, listPets))
mux.Handle("POST /orders", guard.Require(aauth.Access{Level: aauth.AccessPerson}, placeOrder))
mux.Handle("DELETE /pets/{id}", guard.Require(aauth.Access{Level: aauth.AccessAuth, Scope: "pets:write"}, deletePet))
mux.Handle("/", guard.WellKnown()) // metadata and keys

In a handler, aauth.CallerFromContext returns who called: the token type, the agent's key thumbprint (and, from an agent token, its identifier and provider (AgentIssuer, Agent)), the person's (Issuer, Subject) and Tenant, the granted Scope and Account, and the token's JTI.

The guard refuses a request signed for another host (Verify.Signature.Authority defaults to the host of Resource). TrustIssuer names the person servers whose person tokens it accepts, and runs before their keys are fetched. Auth tokens are accepted in three-party only from those person servers, and with Audience set (four-party) only from that access server. Set IsRevoked to refuse tokens their issuer revoked (§11.12): it is asked about every token by (iss, jti).

The operation requires and the request presents The guard answers any level no Signature-Key 401 requirement=agent-token AccessPerson or AccessAuth an agent token 401 requirement=person-token AccessAuth a person token 401 requirement=auth-token with a resource token for the scope AccessAuth an auth token without the scope 401 requirement=auth-token for the token's scope plus the new one any level a token from an issuer TrustIssuer refuses 403

An agent using aauth.Transport answers each challenge itself. The challenge for a missing scope also asks for the scope the agent already holds, because the agent keeps one auth token per resource: the new token replaces the old one without losing access.

docs.title: Ask Only What the Agent Can Answer
docs.text:
Before deferring a request for the person, check that the agent declared it can involve them (§11.7); otherwise refuse, so the agent is not left waiting:

if !aauth.CanRaise(r, aauth.RequirementInteraction) {
    aauth.WriteProblem(w, http.StatusForbidden, aauth.TokenErrUserUnreachable,
        "declare the interaction capability so the person can approve")
    return
}

aauth.CanRequirePayment is the same check before answering 402.

docs.title: Serve an Authorization Endpoint
docs.text: Agents can ask for a scope before calling (§6.6). aauth.AuthorizationHandler verifies the person token and the signature and asks your Decide function. Its required TrustIssuer names the person servers whose person tokens it accepts. Its AuthorizeDecision holds one of: a ResourceToken for the agent to redeem at its person server; a granted Scope, with an optional SessionToken, when the resource authorizes the agent itself; or Pending, to wait for the person first. Publish its URL as authorization_endpoint in the resource metadata. The compile-checked version is the PS authorization step of examples/walkthrough.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
The AAuth sandbox runs every AAuth role from this module on your machine: an agent provider, a person server (PS), an access server (AS) and two demo resources, each on its own HTTPS origin. A signing helper lets HTTP clients that cannot sign, such as Postman, Newman and curl, act as the agent.

The sandbox is a development tool. Its keys, certificate authority and automatic consent are for local use only.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Origin What it does Agent provider https://ap.aauth.test Issues agent tokens: POST /agent-token (two-key refresh, jkt-jwt), POST /enroll (hwk) Person server https://ps.aauth.test Person tokens (POST /person), auth tokens (POST /token), consent at /interaction Access server https://as.aauth.test Auth tokens for docs.aauth.test, federated from the PS (POST /token) Resource https://resource.aauth.test Resource tokens name the PS (three-party) Docs resource https://docs.aauth.test Resource tokens name the AS (four-party)

Each demo resource serves:

Path Access mode GET /api/documents Agent identity (agent token), person identity (person token), or PS and federated authorization (auth token) GET /api/data Resource-managed access: a 202 with an interaction, a poll of Location, then an AAuth-Access session token presented as Authorization: AAuth <token> POST /authorize The authorization endpoint: a signed request presenting a person token, body {"scope": "data.read data.write"}, answered with a resource_token

The scopes offered are documents:read, data.read and data.write.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text:
go install github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go/cmd/aauth-sandbox@latest
aauth-sandbox serve

Server identifiers are https origins without a port (draft-11 §11.1), so the sandbox listens on port 443. macOS lets ordinary users bind it; on Linux, grant CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or run it in a container.

The roles listen on 127.0.0.1:443 and the signing helper on 127.0.0.1:8099, on loopback only. Anyone who can reach the roles can read the trace, which holds every token, and get consent approved automatically; anyone who can reach the helper can sign requests as the test agent. serve refuses a non-loopback --listen or --signer address unless you also pass --listen-any-interface or --signer-any-interface. Use those flags only inside a container whose ports are published on the host's loopback address.

Point the names at your machine, once:

aauth-sandbox hosts | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

The sandbox's own server-to-server requests, and requests through the signing helper, reach the roles without hosts entries. You need them only to open the consent pages in a browser or to call the roles directly.

docs.title: Run It in Docker
docs.text:
Docker runs the sandbox without a Go toolchain. Two Compose files are in deploy/docker/:

File Layout Use it for compose.yaml Every role and the signing helper in one container; port 443 and the helper published on 127.0.0.1 Day-to-day development, Postman, browsers compose.roles.yaml One container per role on a shared network, each answering at its .aauth.test name, plus the helper in its own container Seeing traffic between roles cross a real network; testing a role in isolation 
# Every role in one container
docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml up -d --build --wait

# One container per role
docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.roles.yaml up -d --build --wait

# Drive all five access modes through the signing helper
deploy/docker/smoke.sh http://127.0.0.1:8099
  • Ports. SIGNER_PORT and SANDBOX_HTTPS_PORT change the host ports, for example SIGNER_PORT=8199 docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml up -d. Both are published on 127.0.0.1 only.
  • State. The CA and keys live in a Compose volume, so they survive restarts. docker compose … down -v removes them. With one container per role, an init service creates the CA and every key before the roles start, so they never race to create them.
  • CA certificate. docker compose -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml exec sandbox aauth-sandbox ca export --state /state > aauth-sandbox-ca.pem.
  • Health. Each container's health check is aauth-sandbox health, which asks the roles it serves (and, with --signer, the helper) to answer. The image has no shell or curl.
  • Image. deploy/docker/Dockerfile builds a static binary on a distroless, non-root image: docker build -f deploy/docker/Dockerfile -t aauth-sandbox:dev .

To run the image without Compose, publish its ports on the host's loopback address:

docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:443:443 -p 127.0.0.1:8099:8099 aauth-sandbox:dev

Do not publish them as -p 443:443 -p 8099:8099. Docker then listens on every interface of the host, and anyone on your network can read the trace, get consent approved and sign requests through the helper. Inside the container the sandbox listens on every interface (--listen-any-interface, --signer-any-interface), so the host-side address is the only thing that keeps it local.

The CLI options the Compose files use are available outside Docker too: --roles ps serves only the person server and reaches the other roles at their usual names; --roles none runs only the signing helper; aauth-sandbox init creates the CA and every key ahead of time.

docs.title: Trust the Certificate Authority
docs.text:
On first run the sandbox creates a certificate authority in ~/.aauth-sandbox and a certificate for the role names. Export it and trust it only in the tools that call the sandbox:

aauth-sandbox ca export > aauth-sandbox-ca.pem
  • Postman: Settings > Certificates > CA certificates, then select aauth-sandbox-ca.pem.
  • curl: --cacert aauth-sandbox-ca.pem.
  • Go and other clients: add it to the client's own root pool, as sandbox.NewClient does.
  • Browsers: accept the warning for the consent pages, or trust the CA in a separate browser profile used only for the sandbox.

Avoid adding it to your system trust store. The CA's private key sits unencrypted in the state directory, and every program on the machine would trust what it signs.

The CA is limited to the sandbox's names. Its name constraints let it issue certificates only for the sandbox domain (aauth.test and its subdomains), localhost, any host name you serve outside the domain, and the loopback addresses; clients refuse a certificate it signs for any other site. It is valid for a year.

The sandbox replaces the CA, and logs that it did, when the CA has less than 30 days left, when it has no name constraints (a CA created by an earlier version), or when you serve a host name it does not cover, such as --upstream api.example.dev=.... Export it again and trust the new one wherever you trusted the old. Keep upstream names under the sandbox domain (--upstream petstore=... is petstore.aauth.test) to avoid a new CA.

docs.title: Sign Requests with the Helper
docs.text:
The helper listens on http://127.0.0.1:8099, on loopback only. Send a request to the helper with the target URL as its path; the helper signs it as the sandbox's test agent and forwards it:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8099/https://resource.aauth.test/api/documents

Control headers, removed before forwarding:

Header Values X-Sandbox-Present agent (default): the agent token; person or auth: the token in X-Sandbox-Token; hwk; jkt-jwt: a naming JWT from the agent's durable key; none: forward unsigned X-Sandbox-Token The token to present. For agent it replaces the helper's own agent token X-Sandbox-Capabilities The capabilities the agent declares (default interaction; empty for none)

Without X-Sandbox-Present or X-Sandbox-Token, the helper signs as the request's own Signature-Key says, the way a signing proxy receives requests from clients that cannot sign, such as Postman collections that pidl generates with --signer proxy:

Signature-Key received The helper sig=jwt;jwt="<token>" Presents the token as the agent, person or auth token its typ names sig=jwt, or none Presents its own agent token sig=hwk, sig=jkt-jwt Signs with that scheme

The helper adds Content-Digest to bodies and signs @method, @authority, @path, signature-key, and content-digest, content-type and authorization when present. It declares the agent's capabilities as AAuth-Capabilities to the resources, and as a capabilities member in JSON bodies sent to the PS when the body has none. Responses come back unchanged.

POST /sign with {"method", "url", "headers": [[name, value]], "body", "present", "token"} returns the headers to add, for clients that send requests themselves.

The helper is for tools on your machine, not for web pages:

  • Hosts it answers at. It answers only when the request's Host is localhost, a loopback address or the address it listens on. That keeps a web page from reaching it through a DNS name pointed at 127.0.0.1. Add another name with --signer-host, for example the service name another container uses to reach it.
  • Browser requests. It refuses requests that carry Origin, or Sec-Fetch-Site set to cross-site or same-site, which browsers add for requests made by web pages. curl, Postman and Newman send neither. It answers OPTIONS itself and does not forward it.
  • Targets. It signs and forwards only to the sandbox's role origins, including --remote ones, and its --upstream hosts. Pass --signer-any-target to serve to sign for any https host.
  • Redirects. It returns a redirect to you as it received it and never follows it, so a signed request goes only to the URL you named.

docs.title: A Full Flow with curl
docs.text:
H=http://127.0.0.1:8099

# Agent token (two-key refresh)
AT=$(curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Sandbox-Present: jkt-jwt' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}' \
  $H/https://ap.aauth.test/agent-token | jq -r .agent_token)

# Person token for the resource
PT=$(curl -s -X POST -H "X-Sandbox-Token: $AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"resource": "https://resource.aauth.test"}' $H/https://ps.aauth.test/person | jq -r .person_token)

# Resource token from the authorization endpoint
RT=$(curl -s -X POST -H 'X-Sandbox-Present: person' -H "X-Sandbox-Token: $PT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"scope": "data.read data.write"}' $H/https://resource.aauth.test/authorize | jq -r .resource_token)

# Auth token from the PS; consent is automatic
AUTH=$(curl -s -X POST -H "X-Sandbox-Token: $AT" -H 'Prefer: wait=10' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"resource_token\": \"$RT\", \"presented_token\": \"$PT\"}" $H/https://ps.aauth.test/token | jq -r .auth_token)

# Call the API with the auth token
curl -s -H 'X-Sandbox-Present: auth' -H "X-Sandbox-Token: $AUTH" $H/https://resource.aauth.test/api/documents

If the token request answers 202, follow its Location with GET, signed as the agent, until it answers 200. Location values are absolute URLs.

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
--consent auto (the default) approves every interaction for --person (default alice) as soon as it is created. With --consent manual, open the url of the AAuth-Requirement in a browser and approve, or approve headlessly:

curl -X POST "https://ps.aauth.test/sandbox/approve?code=ABCD-EFGH" --cacert aauth-sandbox-ca.pem

docs.title: Trace
docs.text:
Every message the local roles send and receive is recorded, including the PS-to-AS federation that a client never sees:

aauth-sandbox trace          # print
aauth-sandbox trace --clear  # clear

The same list is at GET https://<any role host>/sandbox/trace; DELETE clears it. The trace holds every token the roles exchanged, so it refuses requests from web pages (those carrying Origin, or Sec-Fetch-Site set to cross-site or same-site). Opening it directly in a browser works.

docs.title: Test Another Implementation
docs.text:
Replace a role with an external implementation with --remote:

aauth-sandbox serve --remote ps=https://ps.example.com

The sandbox stops serving that role and calls the external origin instead: agent tokens name it as the agent's PS, and resources name it as the audience of their resource tokens. The signing helper signs for the external origin too.

docs.title: Front Your Own Server
docs.text:
Run a resource you are developing behind the sandbox with --upstream:

petstore-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 &
aauth-sandbox serve --upstream petstore=http://127.0.0.1:8080

The sandbox serves https://petstore.aauth.test with its CA and passes each request to the server with its Host header, so the server's identifier is https://petstore.aauth.test and signatures over @authority still verify. Its traffic appears in the trace, and the signing helper reaches it like a role. Add the name to your hosts entry (aauth-sandbox hosts --upstream petstore=... prints it). The server itself fetches the PS's keys from https://ps.aauth.test, so it must trust the sandbox CA.

An agent of your own enrolls at the sandbox's agent provider with agentprovider.Client.Enroll, then calls the server through aauth.Transport:

ap := &agentprovider.Client{BaseURL: "https://ap.aauth.test",
    Paths: agentprovider.Paths{Token: sandbox.PathEnroll}, HTTPClient: hc}
agent, err := ap.Enroll(ctx, key, nil)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
ps := aauth.NewPSClient(agent.PS, agent)
ps.HTTPClient = hc
client := &http.Client{Transport: aauth.NewTransport(agent, ps)}
res, err := client.Get("https://petstore.aauth.test/pets")

docs.title: State
docs.text: ~/.aauth-sandbox (or --state) holds the CA (ca.pem, ca-key.pem) and each role's key under keys/. Keys persist across restarts, so tokens and thumbprints stay stable. Delete the directory to start over.

docs.title: Hosted AP, PS, and AS
docs.text:
The server roles are http.Handlers over interfaces you implement: storage (personserver.Store, accessserver.Store) and policy (personserver.Decider, accessserver.Authorizer, and the optional MissionApprover, PermissionDecider, InteractionRelay, and agentprovider.Registrar). The library never decides policy. A decision allows, denies, or defers, and the hosting application resolves deferred requests from its own approval UI (Approve, Deny, Ask).

One origin can host all three roles (PS-AS collapse, §9.3.3); each keeps its own key, metadata document, and JWKS:

ap, err := agentprovider.New(agentprovider.Config{
    Issuer: issuer, Key: apKey,
    Limiter: ratelimit.Per(10, time.Minute),
})

as, err := accessserver.New(accessserver.Config{
    Issuer: issuer, Key: asKey,
    Store: accessserver.NewMemoryStore(), // your database in production
    Authorizer: accessserver.AuthorizerFunc(func(ctx context.Context, r *accessserver.AuthorizationRequest) (accessserver.Decision, error) {
        return accessserver.Allow(""), nil // the resource token's scope
    }),
    Limiter: ratelimit.Per(5, time.Second),
})

ps, err := personserver.New(personserver.Config{
    Issuer: issuer, Key: psKey,
    SubjectKey:     subjectKey, // 32+ random bytes, kept stable
    Store:          personserver.NewMemoryStore(),
    InteractionURL: issuer + "/consent",
    Decider: personserver.DeciderFunc(func(ctx context.Context, r *personserver.TokenRequest) (personserver.Decision, error) {
        switch {
        case r.Person == "":
            return personserver.DeferInteraction(), nil // a new agent: the person signs in at /consent
        case r.Chained && r.Mission == nil:
            return personserver.DeferApproval(), nil // call chaining: ask the person
        }
        return personserver.Allow(personserver.Grant{}), nil
    }),
    Federator:    as.Local(issuer), // in-process PS-AS federation
    CollocatedAS: func(resource string) bool { return resource == "https://ledger.example" },
    Limiter:      ratelimit.Per(5, time.Second),
})

mux := http.NewServeMux()
ap.Register(mux)
ps.Register(mux)
as.Register(mux)

The consent page passes the ?code= it receives to ps.LookupCode to show the request; looking a code up does not consume it, so a link preview cannot burn it. At the decision the page authenticates the person, consumes the code as that person with ps.ConsumeCode, and calls ps.Approve with a Grant naming the person, which binds the agent, and the Revision of the request it showed: if the agent replaced the request meanwhile, Approve fails with ErrRequestChanged. Code attempts are rate-limited per client key (the browser's session or address) when a Limiter is configured. ap.IssueAgentToken issues tokens for agent keys the application has authorized. The PS routes live under /ps/ by default, so agents find them with PSClient.Discover. The full, compile-checked version is Example_collapsedDeployment, and the e2e test runs the whole flow: enrollment, three-party access, missions, PS-AS collapse, audit, and a revocation cascade.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
go test -race ./...
golangci-lint run

Unit tests cover token round trips and rejections, signature tampering, replay guards, delegation rules, JWKS caching, and every server endpoint against live httptest servers, and the e2e package runs every role together (below). Runnable Example functions double as API documentation.

docs.title: End-to-end tests
docs.text:
The e2e package runs the roles together on httptest servers with in-memory stores and seeded policy, so it needs no network, database, or credentials and runs the same locally and in CI. Each deployment has an agent provider and person server on one origin, two resources, and an enrolled agent whose key a work session registered. Resource A uses the person server directly (three-party); resource B uses an access server. The two tests differ in where that access server runs:

Test Topology Federation TestCollapsedDeployment Agent provider, person server, and access server on one origin (§9.3.3) In-process (Server.Local) TestFourPartyDeployment Access server on its own origin (§9.1) Over HTTP (accessserver.Client), signed as the PS; the test checks that requests reached the AS's token and revocation endpoints

Both run the same scenario as subtests, in order, each skipped if an earlier one failed:

  1. three-party access at A, where Alice's approval binds the agent to her;
  2. propose a mission;
  3. B refuses a request outside a mission;
  4. access at B under the mission, with the access server's deferred approval;
  5. audit, update, and completion of the mission, checking the mission log;
  6. revocation of the agent token, cascading to both resources;
  7. the revoked agent obtains nothing new.

Run one topology, with the steps listed:

go test -race -v -run TestFourPartyDeployment ./e2e

Each step logs a plain-English summary of its flow. To also see the HTTP calls between the agent, resources, and servers, set AAUTH_E2E_TRACE=1:

AAUTH_E2E_TRACE=1 go test -v -run TestFourPartyDeployment ./e2e

trace: #41  agent     GET B/ledger
trace: #41            -> 401  AAuth-Requirement: requirement=person-token
trace: #42  agent     POST AP+PS/ps/person
trace: #42            -> 200
trace: #43  agent     GET B/ledger
trace: #43            -> 401  AAuth-Requirement: requirement=auth-token; resource-token="eyJhbGci…"
trace: #44  agent     POST AP+PS/ps/token
trace: #45  PS        POST AS/as/token
trace: #45            -> 200
trace: #44            -> 200
trace: #46  agent     GET B/ledger
trace: #46            -> 200

Each call has a number and logs when it starts and when it returns. A call made while handling another, such as the PS calling the AS to answer the agent's /ps/token request (#45 inside #44), starts and ends between the outer call's two lines. Parties are named by role (agent, AP+PS, AS, and the resources A and B).

AAUTH_E2E_TRACE=1 shows the protocol calls: tokens, challenges, federation, and revocation. AAUTH_E2E_TRACE=2 adds the metadata and key-set fetches each party makes to learn how to verify or reach another, marked (discovery), which are about half of all requests.

The e2e workflow runs the two topologies as separate jobs with the trace at level 1, and each job's summary lists its steps, so the Actions logs show which flow each job exercises.

Wire-format golden vectors live in testdata/vectors: language-neutral JSON (JWK thumbprints, identifiers, header codecs, metadata documents, deterministic Ed25519 JWTs, RFC 9421 request signatures) that another implementation can run as a conformance check. After an intentional wire change, regenerate the derived values and review the diff:

go test -run TestVectors -update

docs.text:

docs.title: v0.1.0
docs.text:
Released 2026-07-07.

The initial implementation of draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-09.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Agent identity and tokens.
  • HTTP message signatures.
  • The three-party token exchange.
  • The agent Transport, which answers challenges and retries.
  • Permission and audit endpoints.
  • Call chaining, clarification chat, and interaction chaining.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: v0.2.0 implements a later draft and is not wire-compatible with v0.1. See Migrating from v0.1.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The module path became github.com/aauth-dev/auth-go.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: The repository was later renamed to aauth-go, and v0.2.0 uses the module path github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go. Imports of the v0.1.1 path must change when you move to v0.2.0; see v0.2.0.

docs.title: v0.2.0
docs.text:
Released 2026-10-09.

v0.2.0 tracks draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11, draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-09, and draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap-02 (previously -09, -04, and -01). Draft -11 changes the wire format, so v0.1 and v0.2 parties cannot talk to each other.

docs.title: Upgrade first
docs.text:
1. Upgrade every agent, resource, and server you operate together. Mixed versions do not interoperate.

  2. Change the module path. The repository was renamed from auth-go to aauth-go:

    // v0.1
import aauth "github.com/aauth-dev/auth-go"

// v0.2
import aauth "github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go"

    go get github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go@v0.2.0

  3. Use Go 1.26 or later (was 1.24).

  4. Work through the breaking changes in Migrating from v0.1, which has before and after code for each.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Every role in one module. New packages personserver, accessserver, agentprovider, and ratelimit join the root aauth package. Each server is an http.Handler over storage and policy interfaces you implement.
  • Person tokens, missions, and permissions. PSClient can request person tokens, propose and complete missions, and ask for permission, and Transport answers person-token challenges.
  • ES256 alongside Ed25519, with keys as crypto.Signer, so platform keystores and HSMs work.
  • Federation. Four-party access through a Federator, and in-process PS-AS collapse with accessserver.Server.Local.
  • Token revocation with cascade, in every server role.
  • Rate limiting through the Limiter interface.
  • Conformance vectors under testdata/vectors for other implementations.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Metadata issuer must match the URL it was fetched from, and issuers must be server identifiers before any discovery fetch.
  • JWKS and metadata responses are bounded in size, and the JWKS cache bounds refetch rate and entry count.
  • Discovery, revocation delivery, and federation use DiscoveryClient when no client is configured. It allows only https and public unicast destinations, including on redirects.
  • Rate limits cover interaction code attempts, polling, revocations, issuance, and new resources per agent.
  • An auth token issued while its grant was being revoked could stay usable until it expired. Recording an auth token now refuses, atomically with revocation, to proceed against a revoked presented token, root person token, or terminated mission.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: The changelog lists every addition, breaking change, removal, and fix.

docs.title: v0.3.0
docs.text:
Released 2026-10-26.

v0.3.0 still tracks draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11, draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-09, and draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap-02. The wire format is unchanged, so v0.2 and v0.3 parties interoperate. v0.3 verifies more strictly, so it refuses some requests v0.2 accepted; see Security.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
go get github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go@v0.3.0

Go 1.26 or later, as for v0.2. Some APIs change, mostly in the server packages: approvals carry the revision of the request shown, interaction codes are looked up and then consumed at the person's decision, the ClaimsProvider takes a request, and stores gain pruning and counting methods. AuthorizationHandler requires TrustIssuer, and an agent provider's Domain must be its issuer's host. The migration guide lists every change with before and after code.

accessserver.Client now reports an access server's 402 Payment Required as an error wrapping *aauth.PaymentRequiredError when no Payment handler is configured.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
These change the API, so code using them needs updating to compile:

  • personserver: ConsumeCodeFor is removed; LookupCode(ctx, code, client) shows a request and ConsumeCode(ctx, code, client, person) consumes its code at the person's decision. ClaimsProvider takes a *ClaimsRequest. Store gains Prune, TokenStore gains CountRevocations and PendingStore gains CountOpenPending.
  • accessserver: Approve(ctx, id, revision, scope) and ConsumeCode(ctx, code, client, person). Store gains CountOpenPending, CountRevocations and Prune.
  • sandbox: LoadOrCreateCA takes optional domains, and Signer is no longer comparable.

These compile unchanged but now fail or refuse what v0.2 accepted:

  • AuthorizationHandler answers 500 until TrustIssuer is set.
  • NewResourceGuard fails when Resource has no host. In four-party mode the guard takes auth tokens only from Audience, so TrustIssuer lists person servers only.
  • personserver.Approve fails with ErrRequestChanged for a request the agent updated unless Grant.Revision names the revision shown.
  • agentprovider.New fails when Config.Domain is not the issuer's host, and verifiers refuse an agent token whose sub is outside its iss domain.
  • SelfSignedResolver verifies only top-level agent tokens.
  • Agent tokens over 24 hours and resource tokens over 5 minutes are refused (MaxLifetime), as are request bodies over 4 MiB during verification (MaxBodySize).
  • The person server refuses call chaining unless Config.AllowCallChaining is set.
  • Pending URLs answer 410 Gone after delivering their result once.
  • Problem responses no longer carry internal error text.
  • aauth-sandbox serve listens on 127.0.0.1 unless --listen-any-interface is given, and the signing helper signs only for the sandbox's hosts and upstreams unless --signer-any-target is given. The sandbox replaces its CA on the first run, so trust the new ca.pem again in Postman, curl or your browser profile.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Capabilities. Agents say what they can handle with AAuth-Capabilities (Transport.Capabilities): involving the person, answering clarifications, or paying. Resources check CanRaise and CanRequirePayment before asking, so an agent is never left waiting for a person nobody will ask.
  • Access ahead of a call. Transport.Authorize asks a resource's authorization endpoint for a scope before the first request, and caches the auth token or session token it gets. Resources serve the endpoint with AuthorizationHandler.
  • Payment. A 402 Payment Required carries the payment protocol's challenge in PaymentRequiredError; set Transport.Payment to settle it, and the transport polls or retries afterwards. No payment protocol is built in.
  • ResourceGuard. Each operation of a resource declares the least it needs (AccessAgent, AccessPerson, or AccessAuth with a scope). The guard verifies the presented token, challenges for the next one, and hands the verified Caller to the handler. An auth-token challenge also asks for the scope the agent already holds, so one auth token per resource keeps every grant.
  • Hosted agents in one call. agentprovider.Client.Enroll enrolls a key at an agent provider and returns an aauth.Agent that keeps its tokens fresh.
  • The sandbox. aauth-sandbox runs the agent provider, person server, access server and demo resources for all five access modes on https://*.aauth.test, locally or in Docker, with its own certificate authority, consent pages, a message trace, and a signing helper for clients that cannot sign, such as Postman and curl. The helper also signs as a request's own Signature-Key names, so generic clients need no sandbox headers. --remote swaps in another implementation of a role, and --upstream puts a resource of your own behind it. See the sandbox guide.
  • Walkthrough code. examples/walkthrough has tested code for each step of the AAuth walkthroughs, for every role, marked as named regions that the PIDL walkthrough viewer shows next to the HTTP messages.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
v0.3.0 closes several ways a party could act beyond what it was given.

  • Signatures are bound to the receiving server. Servers and ResourceGuard refuse a request whose signed @authority is another host, so a server an agent calls cannot replay the request to another server. Use RequestVerifyOptions.Authority and AuthorityOf when you verify requests yourself.
  • Four-party resources take auth tokens only from their access server. With ResourceGuardConfig.Audience set, an auth token must be issued by that access server, so a person server cannot skip it.
  • Agent identifiers belong to their provider. An agent token's sub must be in the domain of its iss. SelfSignedResolver verifies only top-level agent tokens.
  • Consent covers what the person saw. An agent cannot widen a request the person approved while an access server decides, and approvals fail with ErrRequestChanged when the request changed after it was shown.
  • Key discovery stays on the issuer. dwk must be one of the four AAuth metadata documents, and redirects to another host are refused.
  • Bounded work for unauthenticated callers. Verification reads at most 4 MiB of a body, the JWKS cache resists floods of unknown issuers, stores are capped and pruned, and rate limits are kept per key space.
  • Less to learn from errors. Responses carry fixed descriptions, not internal error text.
  • Interaction codes are consumed at the person's authenticated decision, limited per client, and refused once expired. Pending URLs answer 410 Gone after delivering their result.
  • Call chaining is opt-in at the person server (Config.AllowCallChaining), and ResourceGuard can check revocation (IsRevoked) and passes the token's account and tenant to the handler.
  • The sandbox stays on your machine. It listens on loopback by default; the signing helper returns redirects unchanged, answers only local clients, refuses browser requests, and signs only for the sandbox's hosts and upstreams; its CA is limited to the sandbox's names; and the image builds with Go 1.27.3.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• ChainInteraction and WriteClarification mark their 202 bodies as JSON.
  • aauth-sandbox serve records its listener address before its first request, which could otherwise dial the default port.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The agent guide covers enrolling at a hosted agent provider, declaring capabilities, requesting access ahead of a call, and paying.
  • The resource guide covers ResourceGuard, checking capabilities, and the authorization endpoint.
  • The new sandbox guide covers running locally and in Docker, the signing helper, the trace, and fronting your own server, and trusting its CA in each tool rather than system-wide.
  • The design and security notes cover signature binding, agent identifiers, four-party issuers and consent revisions.

Every change is in the changelog.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
aauth-go implements the AAuth drafts below. They are works in progress, and each revision can change the wire format; the module's minor version moves with them until the protocol stabilizes.

  • Protocol coverage records, section by section, what this module implements.
  • The protocol itself is specified upstream; this site does not copy it. For an interactive tour, see explorer.aauth.dev.

Section Status Notes §11.1 Identifiers ✅ ValidateServerIdentifier (https, host only, lowercase, A-labels) §11.2 Metadata documents ✅ All four roles; issuer checked against the fetch URL; Validate for REQUIRED members; aauth-resource link relation §11.3 HTTP message signatures ✅ @method @authority @path signature-key, plus content-digest and content-type on bodies; created window and clock_skew; Signature-Key schemes jwt, jwks_uri (server-signed requests), and jkt-jwt and hwk (agent provider only) §11.4 JWKS discovery and caching ✅ Cache headers, one-minute refresh floor, unknown-kid refresh, 24-hour maximum age, backoff, bounded entries §11.5 AAuth tokens ✅ typ and dwk checked first, iat required, exp with no skew, iss a server identifier, one-hour person and auth tokens; Ed25519 and ES256 only §11.6 Requirement responses ✅ AAuth-Requirement as an RFC 9651 dictionary with all seven values §11.7 AAuth-Capabilities header ✅ Transport.Capabilities (unioned with MissionCapabilities) sent on requests to resources and as the PS capabilities parameter; RequestCapabilities and CanRaise for resources §11.8 Deferred responses ✅ 202, Location, Retry-After, Prefer: wait, 429 backoff; 402 settled through a PaymentHandler, then Location polled (§11.8.4) §11.9 Error responses ✅ signature-key-09 Signature-Error codes; RFC 9457 problem bodies; token endpoint and polling error codes §11.10, §11.11 Scopes and account binding ✅ Scope never broader than requested; account carried through §11.12 Token revocation ✅ RevocationClient; recipients in every server role, with cascade and downstream outcomes

docs.title: PLAN — aauth-go v0.3.0
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-AAUTHGO-001

docs.title: Build Order
docs.text:
1. Protocol-11 gaps: capabilities, authorization endpoint, mission termination helpers, payment. Small and independent; capabilities first because payment and R3 use it.
  2. Bootstrap: coverage table first (it confirms the gap list), then key rotation, operator helper, nonces.
  3. R3 foundation: types, hashing, documents, token claims, issuer checks, authorization with operations.
  4. R3 enforcement: matchers, per-call proposals, single-use grants.
  5. Samples and trace: walkthrough regions for existing scenarios can start early, since they use v0.2 APIs; R3 and bootstrap regions follow their features.
  6. Release: coverage tables, changelog, migration notes, release notes; tag after CI passes.

docs.text: Risk Mitigation R3 is a -00 draft and may change Isolate in package r3; phase enforcement separately Region names drift and break PIDL samples Names listed in doc.go; a test fails if a listed region is missing Trace includes values that change per run Volatile pointers; role-named hosts Payment semantics depend on rails Opaque data plus a hook; no rail code

docs.text: PIDL's AAuth content (INIT-PIDL-004) quotes the walkthrough regions as Go samples and checks its HTTP examples against the JSON trace.

docs.title: PRD — aauth-go v0.3.0
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-AAUTHGO-001 Repository: github.com/aauth-dev/aauth-go

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
v0.2.0 implements nearly all of draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11, draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-09 and draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap-02. The remaining gaps block complete AAuth walkthroughs and real deployments:

  • Protocol-11: no agent-side client for the resource authorization endpoint (§6.6); AAuth-Capabilities is never sent (§11.7); a 402 payment response is only reported as an error (§6.5, §9.1.2, §11.8).
  • Bootstrap-02: an agent cannot rotate its ephemeral key with each refresh (§8.1), one operator cannot run many self-hosted agents (§4.3.1), and there is no attestation nonce helper (§8.3, §11.4). The README has no bootstrap coverage table.
  • Rich Resource Requests (draft-hardt-aauth-r3-00) are not implemented.
  • Teaching material: Transport hides the protocol's messages inside one hc.Get, which is right for applications but cannot show a learner each step. Walkthroughs (such as PIDL's AAuth viewer) need small, tested Go snippets per step and a record of the real HTTP traffic to check their examples against.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Close every implementable gap in the three drafts v0.2.0 targets, and add R3.
  • Provide tested, step-sized Go samples for every AAuth walkthrough scenario, marked so documentation tools can quote them.
  • Export the end-to-end test traffic as JSON so documentation examples can be checked against what the SDK actually sends.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• The Signature-Key x509 scheme. Protocol-11 requires agents to sign with jwt and servers with jwks_uri (§11.3.2), and a server answers any other scheme with unsupported_scheme. x509 has no role in AAuth-11; it may come later as a separate package for non-AAuth use.
  • A mission control plane endpoint. §8.6 leaves status, termination and delegation queries to a companion specification that does not exist yet; an invented endpoint would not interoperate.
  • Payment rails (x402, card networks, settlement). The SDK carries the protocol shape and a hook; rails are integrations.
  • Vendor attestation implementations (platform-specific verifiers stay behind AttestationVerifier).

docs.title: Protocol-11
docs.text:
1. Capabilities (§11.7). Constants for interaction, clarification and payment; formatting and parsing of the RFC 9651 list; Transport sends AAuth-Capabilities on signed requests to resources, as the union of the agent's capabilities and the mission's approved capabilities; resources can read the header, and the challenge helpers do not raise interaction to an agent that did not declare it.
  2. Authorization endpoint (§6.6). An agent-side Authorize that sends the signed request with a person token and scope (and account), and handles each outcome: authorized (with an optional AAuth-Access session token), a deferred interaction, or a resource token that it verifies (§6.7.3) and exchanges at the PS; errors map to problem types (invalid_request, invalid_scope, invalid_account). A resource-side handler helper decides over verified person claims.
  3. Mission termination (§8.6, §8.8). MissionStatusError exposes the termination reason, keeps unknown reasons opaque, and says whether re-proposal makes sense (expired, superseded) or not (revoked); mission_control_endpoint is carried in PS metadata.
  4. Payment (§6.5, §9.1.2, §11.6, §11.8.4, §7.6.1). A PaymentRequiredError carrying Location, the AAuth-Requirement, WWW-Authenticate: Payment challenges and an x402 body as opaque data; a PaymentHandler hook that Transport and the PS federator call before polling Location; interaction requests of type payment; a per-AS billing hook on the PS.

docs.title: Bootstrap-02
docs.text:
1. Coverage table for bootstrap-02 in the README and docs/specs/protocol-coverage.md, like protocol-11's.
  2. Key rotation on refresh (§8.1). A token source that generates a new ephemeral key per two-key refresh and switches the agent's signing key and token together; person and auth tokens bound to the old key are dropped (§8.5).
  3. Many agents, one operator (§4.3.1). A self-hosted helper that issues one agent token per agent key under a separate provider key that is never an agent key.
  4. Attestation nonces (§8.3, §11.4). Single-use nonces with a five-minute maximum lifetime, issued and checked by the agent provider for enrollment and re-attestation.

docs.title: Rich Resource Requests (draft-hardt-aauth-r3-00)
docs.text:
1. Types and discovery: R3 documents, operations for the seven vocabularies (mcp, openapi, grpc, graphql, asyncapi, wsdl, odata), r3_vocabularies in resource metadata, the per-call access mode, and r3_s256 over served bytes.
  2. Documents: a byte-pinned document store and handler that serves only to an AS or PS signing under jwks_uri and entitled by the resource token; a fetch that checks the digest.
  3. Tokens: r3_uri and r3_s256 on resource tokens; r3_uri, r3_s256, r3_granted and r3_per_call on auth tokens. Issuers verify the hash, record an audit entry with issuance, and may narrow the grant; in four-party access the PS checks the AS's R3 claims against the resource token and the document.
  4. Authorization: Authorize accepts r3_operations instead of, or with, scope; resources validate requested operations and compose one document across definitions.
  5. Enforcement: resources decide per call: granted, per-call, or denied. Per-call operations produce a proposal (an R3 document with parameter digests and display detail); per-call grants are single-use and their parameters are compared structurally.

docs.title: Samples and Traces
docs.text:
1. docs.text:
const (

    CapabilityClarification = "clarification"
    CapabilityPayment       = "payment"

docs.title: 2. Authorization Endpoint

type AuthorizeRequest struct {
    Scope        string
    Account      string
    R3Operations *r3.Operations
}
type AuthorizeResult struct {
    Status       string // "authorized"
    Scope        string
    SessionToken string // AAuth-Access, when issued
    AuthToken    string // when the resource returned a resource token and the exchange completed
}
func (t *Transport) Authorize(ctx context.Context, resource string, req AuthorizeRequest) (*AuthorizeResult, error)
func AuthorizationHandler(self string, verify TokenVerifyOptions, decide func(context.Context, *PersonClaims, AuthorizeRequest) (AuthorizeDecision, error)) http.Handler

The endpoint comes from resource metadata (authorization_endpoint). Authorize obtains the person token through the PS client, follows 202 interaction, verifies a returned resource token per §6.7.3, and exchanges it.

docs.title: 4. Payment
docs.text:
type PaymentRequiredError struct {
    Location        string
    Requirement     *Requirement
    WWWAuthenticate []string        // Payment challenges, unparsed beyond auth-params
    X402            json.RawMessage // opaque
}
type PaymentHandler interface {
    Settle(ctx context.Context, p *PaymentRequiredError) error
}

Transport and personserver (as federator) call Settle, then poll Location through the existing deferred loop. Without a handler the error is returned. RequestInteraction accepts Type: "payment".

docs.title: 5. Bootstrap
docs.text:
• agentprovider.RotatingAgent: holds the durable key, creates an ephemeral key per refresh, and swaps {key, agent token} atomically; Transport reads both from it. The PS client's per-key caches drop tokens for retired keys.
  • aauth.Operator: a provider key plus IssueAgentToken(agentPub, name) for many self-hosted agents; refuses the provider key as an agent key.
  • agentprovider.NonceStore with Issue and Consume (single use, at most five minutes); AttestationVerifier receives the nonce.

docs.title: 6. R3
docs.text:
// package r3
type Operations struct {
    Vocabulary string            `json:"vocabulary"`
    Operations []json.RawMessage `json:"operations"` // shape per vocabulary
}
type Document struct {
    Vocabulary string            `json:"vocabulary"`
    Operations []json.RawMessage `json:"operations"`
    Account    string            `json:"account,omitempty"`
    Display    Display           `json:"display"`
    Parameters map[string]Digest `json:"parameters,omitempty"` // per-call proposals
    Result     *Digest           `json:"result,omitempty"`
}
type Digest struct{ S256, Excerpt, MediaType string }
func Hash(served []byte) string                               // base64url SHA-256
type Store interface { Put(doc []byte) (uri, s256 string, err error); Get(uri string) ([]byte, error) }
func Handler(store Store, entitled func(ctx context.Context, signer string, uri string) bool) http.Handler
func Fetch(ctx context.Context, signer aauth.ServerSigner, uri, s256 string) (*Document, []byte, error)
type Matcher interface { Match(granted []json.RawMessage, op json.RawMessage) bool } // one per vocabulary
func Enforce(claims *aauth.AuthClaims, op json.RawMessage, m Matcher) Decision      // Granted | PerCall | Deny
  • Bytes are stored exactly as served; there is no canonicalization.
  • The handler requires VerifyServerRequest and refuses agents.
  • Claims: ResourceTokenParams.R3URI/R3S256; AuthClaims.R3URI/R3S256/R3Granted/R3PerCall. PS and AS issuers verify the digest, call an audit hook in the same step as issuance, and may narrow r3_granted.
  • Per-call: the resource stores a proposal, returns it in the challenge, and consumes a matching single-use grant; parameter comparison is structural (JSON value equality), with digests checked.
